Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data
summary:
Croplytics is a crop-rotation planner built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge "Adapting Farms with NASA Data." Farmers face more frequent droughts, floods and soil loss. In BC, forage farms in the Salmon River valley were ordered to stop irrigating in 2023, 2025 and 2026, often with little warning. Croplytics uses 25 years of NASA satellite data to show a farmer how their own field has behaved: when it sits bare, and when the crop was stressed. It then compares the current rotation with three alternatives on water use, erosion, soil health, nitrogen, forage value and market fit. Farmers set their priorities with sliders and get a plain-language brief for each option, with its evidence, its benefits and what a local expert should double-check.

Behind it are two AI models trained on real data. One detects bare fields and crop seasons, with 98% agreement with Sentinel-2 labels. The other flags crop-stress weeks, and its two methods agree 90% of the time. It found that an irrigated field can stay healthy even when regional drought maps show severe drought. The tool is built on two California example farms, where ground data is richest for checking the satellite results, and BC is the motivating story in the pitch. The guiding principle is that it supports farmers' judgment and never replaces it, and every number shows where it came from.
details:
Croplytics is a decision-support tool that helps farmers explore crop rotations that protect their soil and use water wisely as conditions change. A farmer picks their field and sees 25 years of its history, rebuilt from NASA and partner Earth observations: when the field sits bare and exposed to erosion, when crops green up and are harvested, and which weeks the current crop showed signs of stress. The tool then compares the existing rotation with three alternatives. It scores each one on water use, erosion reduction, organic matter, nitrogen fixing, forage value, pest-cycle breaks and market fit, and shows a range for every score so uncertainty is always visible. Farmers adjust sliders to weight what matters most to them. Each strategy comes with a plain-language brief explaining why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, its benefits, where information is missing, and which risks need review by the farmer or a local agrologist.

The benefit is foresight. Farmers often find out about water stress too late: in British Columbia's Salmon River valley, forage farmers were ordered to stop irrigating in 2023, 2025 and 2026, often with little notice. Croplytics turns decades of free satellite data into field-level insight, so farmers and advisors can plan rotations before the next drought or flood instead of reacting to it. The intended impact is healthier soil, less wasted water, lower erosion risk and more resilient farm incomes, with the tool always supporting local expertise rather than replacing it.

We built the data pipelines, AI models and backend API in Python, using pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, SciPy and matplotlib. The interactive map frontend uses TypeScript, React, Vite and MapLibre. The data comes from NASA POWER weather, MODIS vegetation and land-surface temperature, SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, the Evaporative Stress Index, Landsat, ESA Sentinel-2 imagery, and the USDA Cropland Data Layer and soil surveys. We reached it through public, no-login APIs (NASA, Microsoft Planetary Computer, Earth Search and NASA SERVIR ClimateSERV) and NASA Earthdata AppEEARS. No special hardware is needed; the tool runs in a web browser.

Two AI models run behind the tool. The bare-field detector compares a simple vegetation-index rule against random forest and gradient boosting models. The machine-learning models reached 98% agreement with Sentinel-2 land-cover labels on years they never trained on, against 92% for the rule, and estimated green-up and harvest dates within about five days. The crop-stress detector combines six satellite signals and compares a transparent z-score method with an isolation forest; the two agree on 90% of weeks.

What makes Croplytics creative is that it doesn't hide its AI. It shows simple and machine-learning methods side by side, along with where they disagree. That openness produced one of our most interesting findings: during California's 2021 drought, regional drought indicators were severe, yet our irrigated rice field stayed healthy, showing that coarse drought maps can't see individual fields the way Croplytics can. Every number on screen traces back to its data source.

Throughout the project we put farmers first, using plain language, dual units and an interface that doesn't require geospatial training. We were honest about uncertainty: satellite labels are not ground truth, so we show accuracy, ranges and known limits openly. We tested the models on years they never saw, and checked them against known events such as a 2022 fallow year and the 2021 drought. We built on California example farms, where ground data is richest for validating satellite results, with BC as our motivating case and next step. Above all, we designed Croplytics to support, never replace, the judgment of farmers and local agricultural experts.

Try it live: https://croplytics.xyz — Demo video: https://youtu.be/L0BRtubUIH0
